title: Implementation
body:
The implementation is **how the promise is kept**: the private data members and the bodies of
the member functions. Everything the [[Interface]] deliberately does not say.

In C++ it is the `private` section plus a separate `.cpp` file:

```c++
// intstack.cpp
#include "intstack.h"

IntStack::IntStack() { top = -1; }

bool IntStack::push(int item) {
	if (isFull()) return false;
	data[++top] = item;
	return true;
}
```

The `IntStack::` prefix says which class the function belongs to; without it you have written
a free [[Function]], not a [[Method]].

The rule that makes the split worth anything: **the implementation can change and the client
cannot tell.** Swap the fixed [[Array]] for a [[Linked List]] of [[Node]]s, and every program
using `IntStack` still compiles and still works, because none of them ever mentioned `data` or
`top`. If changing the implementation breaks a client, either the interface leaked or the
client cheated.

That is the reason for `private`. It is not secrecy, it is a promise you are not making. Data
members are private so that no client can come to depend on them, which is what would take
away your freedom to change them later. See [[Encapsulation]].

The same argument, generalised, is [[Coupling and Cohesion]] in
[[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]], where the interface/implementation split is how you
get data coupling instead of content coupling.
